claims.text: The modified alloy is equiatomic FeNiCrMn and contains no Co.
Equiatomic FeNiCrMn can be obtained as a single-phase solid solution by conventional melting or powder metallurgy.
Removing Co from equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi lowers the stacking-fault energy.
Lower testing temperatures promote deformation twinning in Co-free FeNiCrMn.
Higher strain rates promote deformation twinning in Co-free FeNiCrMn.
Deformation twins provide additional plastic-strain accommodation and improve the strength–ductility balance.
At higher temperatures or slower strain rates, dislocation slip dominates and the twin-mediated benefit becomes less pronounced.
Under low-temperature, high-strain-rate conditions, Co-free FeNiCrMn will develop a higher twin density than equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi.
The predicted increase in twin density will correlate with increased ductility and/or delayed strain localization.
Equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi is the Cantor alloy.
The Cantor alloy usually forms a chemically disordered FCC solid solution below its solidus at ambient pressure.
The Cantor alloy exhibits an enhanced strength–ductility combination as temperature decreases.
The low-temperature mechanical response of the Cantor alloy is closely related to deformation-induced nanotwins and stacking faults.
Cantor-alloy deformation is dominated by dislocation slip with only occasional nanotwin formation.
The proposed mechanism is restricted primarily to the solid-solution regime where twinning competes with dislocation glide.
Elevated temperature or very low strain rate can suppress the proposed twinning mechanism through thermal activation.

Failure to observe a statistically significant twin-density increase together with associated mechanical improvement in Co-free FeNiCrMn relative to the Cantor alloy would falsify the proposed mechanism.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis repeatedly invokes high-rate or dynamic loading, but the largest specified experimental strain rate is 10^-2 s^-1, which is generally not a high-rate dynamic regime. Thus the proposed comparison does not clearly test the stated high-strain-rate mechanism.
